analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment firms that own large numbers of single-family rental homes and spends the revenue on down-payment help.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the 118th Congress and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a 50% tax on any new single-family home bought by investment entities that pool money from outside investors, and an annual $50,000-per-home tax on homes those entities own beyond shrinking yearly limits. For investment firms managing $50 million or more, the limit phases down to zero over about nine years, effectively requiring them to sell off single-family rental homes. The tax revenue would go into a new Housing Downpayment Trust Fund that HUD would use to make grants to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance, with priority for families buying homes sold off under the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to buy their first home. The bill pressures large investment firms to sell single-family rentals (sales to people who already own a home or to other businesses don't count toward compliance), which could put more houses on the market for owner-occupants, and it funds down-payment grants to help families close the deal.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on any single-family residence newly acquired by an investment entity that pools outside investors' money, discouraging further corporate buying of homes [S3].

Charges applicable taxpayers $50,000 per year for each single-family residence they own above a cap that shrinks 10% annually; for hedge fund taxpayers (those with $50 million or more in assets under management), the cap reaches zero, requiring divestiture of single-family rentals over roughly nine years [S3].

Routes all revenue from the new taxes into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund, which HUD would use for grants to state housing finance agencies providing down-payment assistance, with priority to families buying homes sold by these investment entities [S3].
Defines a 'disqualified sale' as a sale to another business or to someone who already owns a home, so forced sales must go to first-time or owner-occupant buyers to count [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large investment firms, hedge funds, and real estate investment trusts that own or buy single-family rental homes, which would face acquisition taxes and shrinking ownership caps that force them to sell properties over about nine years. Some of that cost could surface as pressure on rents in markets where those firms own a large share of rentals.

drawbacks.text: The declining ownership caps force large investors to sell off single-family rentals within about nine years; in markets where such firms own a large share of rentals, some analysts would worry about disruption to the rental supply even as sales shift homes to owner-occupants [S3].

The definition of an 'applicable taxpayer' covers any partnership, corporation, or REIT managing pooled investor funds, so it could reach smaller property managers and mom-and-pop partnerships, not just giant hedge funds [S3].
The down-payment grant program only spends what Congress later appropriates from the trust fund, so the assistance is not guaranteed even if the tax collects revenue [S3].
The tax is imposed on acquisition and excess holdings regardless of what the firms charge tenants, so firms could try to pass costs to renters in the short run [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real and growing cost driver for ordinary families — large investors buying up single-family homes — and pairs the stick with direct down-payment help funded by the tax itself. Its main risks are practical: the divestiture timeline could jolt local rental markets, the pooled-fund definition sweeps broadly, and the buyer-assistance side depends on future appropriations. On balance it is a substantial transfer of bargaining power in the housing market back toward individual buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2023 and sent to two committees, the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, but neither took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Smith of Washington introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, joined by Reps. Sanchez and Williams of Georgia as original cosponsors [S3].
Seventeen Democratic cosponsors joined the sponsor; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Financial Services Committee, but the record shows no hearings, markups, committee votes, or floor action [S1][S5].
No further action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by then expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large institutional owners of single-family rentals — hedge funds, private equity firms, and rental REITs — are better off, because they face no acquisition tax, no ownership cap, and no divestiture requirement. Families hoping for more homes on the market and down-payment help gained nothing.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (hedge funds, private equity, rental REITs)
industries.note: The bill puts a 50% tax on their new home purchases, a $50,000-per-home annual tax above shrinking caps, and for the largest firms a full divestiture requirement over about nine years. Their gain from unrestricted home-buying comes at the price of higher purchase costs for ordinary families.

If forced institutional sales and blocked acquisitions shift demand toward owner-occupants, individual buyers become the marginal bidder for homes. Construction and rehabilitation organizations are explicitly exempt from the tax.

industries.industry: State housing finance agencies and mortgage lenders
industries.note: The bill would fund HUD grants to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance programs, and priority for homes sold off by taxed entities, increasing assisted purchase activity.
